attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: 'These' points back to the prompt precision, hallucination and compute-cost barriers named in the previous paragraph. The claim is an unhedged statement about the state of things at publication.

contract.note: Reading 'intractable' as 'still unresolved at publication', not 'permanently impossible', is a fair ordinary reading. Support requires evidence on both the technical and the cost parts. The window of April 1 to May 13, 2024 was chosen by the evaluator but is reasonable.

evidence.note: DW, April 2024: the filmmakers say face consistency, hands and movement were still problems. This supports the technical part only and has no cost data.
OpenAI describing its own product's weaknesses (company disclosure), dated February 2024, before the target period. Background only.

fxguide's cost estimates are explicitly unofficial and set no affordability threshold. The article separates training costs from inference costs. It neither shows nor rules out a prohibitive operating cost.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary evidence backs the technical part: prompt control and consistency problems were still unresolved in April–May 2024. The support condition also requires matched evidence on operating cost, and there is none. The only cost figures are unofficial estimates with no affordability threshold. Nothing shows the barriers were solved either, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The Shy Kids quotes nearby are context, not the claim.

semantics.note: A hyperbolic statement about Sora's workflow at the time. 'If you're making an actual movie' correctly limits the use case. It is not a forecast.

contract.note: The surrounding text is about consistency across shots, so the plain reading, that Sora could not reliably deliver intended, consistent movie scenes without substantial workarounds, is ordinary and fair. A literal 'produces no usable footage' reading would be stretched against him.

evidence.note: fxguide, mid-April 2024, firsthand Shy Kids account: nothing kept shots consistent with each other, the same prompt gave different results, and the balloon sometimes came out the wrong colour or with a face.

A finished music video built from about 55 of roughly 700 clips, with some transitions done in After Effects. It shows some use, plus a high shooting ratio. A stylised music video does not show reliable movie-scene production.

reviews.rationale: Firsthand accounts from the period show the preview had no tools to keep shots consistent, gave different results for the same prompt, and pushed the team into workarounds, such as the balloon head to avoid inconsistent faces. That meets the support condition. Completed stylised projects show partial usefulness at very high retry rates, not reliable scene production, so they do not meet the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own argument, in his own post.

semantics.note: It keeps the 'I would argue' qualifier, 'multiple outlets' and the causal 'let'. But it drops the 'before its announcement' timing, which broadens which coverage counts. 'I would argue' is an assertion, not a probability hedge, so the claim stays causal.

contract.note: Treating the coverage as a material, not sole, cause is fair, and the contract flags the gap between announcement and release openly. It reasonably requires evidence about what buyers knew.

evidence.note: Verge launch-day piece describes the capabilities confidently, but credits the description to Rabbit and notes the demo barely worked. It is announcement-day coverage and says nothing about buyers.
Engadget launch piece repeats Rabbit's pitch but with caveats. Under the contract, caveats in one article do not disprove the claim.
Same outlet and author later sharply criticised the LAM. This supports only the 'now crushing' element.
Engadget's critical review, dated before the post. This supports only the 'now crushing' element.
Rabbit's own post reporting 10,000 units on day one (company disclosure). It counts units, not unique buyers, and says nothing on what buyers read.
A single disappointed buyer quoted. Not representative, and not tied to particular outlets.

reviews.rationale: Two outlets did later criticise the R1, so that part holds. Whether their early coverage 'credulously accepted' the LAM is contested, since both pieces credit the claims to Rabbit and add caveats, and the matched coverage is from launch day, not before the announcement. No purchaser evidence links coverage to about 10,000 poorly informed purchases, so the causal claim is unsettled.
